title: Sartre and Beauvoir
keyWorks: Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions (1939)
summary: Existentialism holds that a human being has no predetermined “essence”: “existence precedes essence,” and we become ourselves through our own choices. Sartre emphasized radical freedom and responsibility; Simone de Beauvoir stressed that freedom is always embodied in a concrete situation and cannot be separated from the freedom of other people.
onEmotions: In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described emotion as a “magical” transformation of the world: when the path of action is blocked, consciousness changes the very way it perceives the situation. For Sartre, an emotion is not something that simply “happens” to us but a way of relating to the world in which we take part. This doesn’t mean a feeling can be switched off by willpower — it means we have freedom in how we live with it. Beauvoir added that feelings are always embedded in a situation — the body, history, relationships — and reflect the “ambiguity” of human existence: we are free and limited at the same time.

anxiety.text: “Man is condemned to be free,” Sartre wrote — and that line describes anxiety better than any definition. If a choice makes you shaky, there is nothing shameful in that. Sartre distinguished fear — of an external threat — from anguish, or anxiety (angoisse): the feeling that arises when we become aware of our own freedom. No one and nothing will decide for you, no instruction manual guarantees the right path, and that can make your head spin. Sartre believed this anxiety is not an illness but a sign that you take your life seriously. Many people hide from it in “bad faith” (mauvaise foi) — the self-deception that there is no choice and everything has been decided for them. Your anxiety is a form of honesty: you see that the future is open. You don’t need to decide everything at once; it is enough to make the next small choice.
anxiety.practice: Stand up and take one step forward, saying to yourself: “I am choosing this step.” Notice that no instruction manual took it for you.

quote.text: Man is condemned to be free.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

fear.text: A wild animal approaches, the legs give way, a person faints — that is one of Sartre’s examples. He saw in it not cowardice but a peculiar cunning of consciousness, and your fear, too, may be trying to protect you. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions he called such fainting “magical” behavior: when we cannot deal with a threat through action, consciousness tries, as it were, to abolish it by cancelling perception itself. Sartre suggested seeing an emotion not as a breakdown but as a way we answer the world. So you can ask: what is this fear trying to do for me? And what actions, however small, are still open to me? Beauvoir would add that fear is always embedded in a situation: sometimes it accurately reflects a real vulnerability in your position — and then the problem lies in the position, not in you.
fear.practice: Question your fear as you would a person: “What are you trying to do for me?” Then get up and do one small action that is still open to you.

sadness.text: When everything fades to gray, Sartre saw not a breakdown but a quiet act of consciousness. If you are sad right now, listen for what it is answering. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described passive sadness like this: when the world demands too much of us, consciousness seems to “dim” it, making everything gray and unimportant — so as to lift an unbearable task from our shoulders for a while. That means sadness is not your failure but a response to a world that is too heavy right now. Beauvoir would remind you of human “ambiguity”: we are free and limited at once, we act and we undergo. Sadness is a moment when the second side is felt more strongly. You can live through it without giving up the first: your freedom hasn’t gone anywhere; it is simply waiting.
sadness.practice: Sit for three minutes in silence, letting the world stay gray. Don’t fix anything — just notice which task your sadness is giving you a break from.

grief.text: In the autumn of 1963 Beauvoir sat by her dying mother’s bed, and no philosophy made it lighter. She knew from the inside the kind of loss you are carrying now. Simone de Beauvoir wrote about it very personally in A Very Easy Death (1964), the book about her mother’s illness and death. She showed that no philosophy makes a loss “reasonable”: the death of someone close is felt as an intrusion and an injustice, even if from the outside it looks “natural.” This matters for existentialism: grief doesn’t need to be justified or explained. Beauvoir also showed that our relationships with others become part of who we are — so a loss changes us too. To accept grief means allowing yourself not to search for meaning in it right away. In time you will find your own way to carry this memory — and that will be your way of keeping the bond.
grief.practice: If you wish, say one sentence out loud to the person who is gone. Not for an answer — so the bond has a voice.

loneliness.text: At the Café de Flore in Paris, Sartre and Beauvoir wrote for years at neighboring tables — each their own work, but side by side. When you are alone and it hurts, their philosophy doesn’t deny it. Sartre believed that in a certain sense everyone is alone before their own freedom: no one can choose for you. He spoke of “abandonment” — we have no ready-made answers handed down from above. But in The Ethics of Ambiguity Beauvoir stressed the other side: my freedom needs the freedom of others. The meanings worth living for are created together, not alone; a person locked inside themselves cannot be truly free. In other words, loneliness is not proof that you aren’t needed but an experience of how deeply you are a creature of connection. You can acknowledge this existential solitude — and still look for people with whom your freedom meets theirs.
loneliness.practice: Send a voice message to someone around whom you feel freer — just ask how their day went.

quote.text: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
quote.author: Simone de Beauvoir

anger.text: The problem won’t come out, and a person tears up the sheet in a fit — that is how Sartre opens his account of anger. Your fury, too, is probably standing before a closed door. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described anger as an attempt to change the world “magically” when the direct path is closed: no way out appears — and we get angry, as if the force of the feeling could replace action. But anger can also be a response to real injustice, to your freedom not being recognized. In The Second Sex Beauvoir showed how the feelings of those whose freedom is restricted are often written off as “temperament” or “nature”. In this light, your anger deserves a hearing: what dead end or what injustice is it pointing to? You have the right to be angry — and the right to decide what to do with that force.
anger.practice: Clench your fists for a count of five, release, and ask: “If my anger could make one demand, what would it be?”

shame.text: A corridor, a keyhole — and suddenly footsteps behind you. This is the most famous scene in Being and Nothingness: a man peeping through a door realizes he has been seen; if you feel ashamed right now, you know that instant from the inside. In that instant he sees himself through another’s eyes — as an object, as “the one who is peeping.” This is “the look of the Other”: another person can see me in a way I cannot see myself, and I have no control over that image. Shame, for Sartre, is the recognition that in some sense I really am the one the other sees. But this is important: you are not reducible to that look. It fixes a moment, while you are a freedom that goes on. Shame shows that you live among people, but it does not define you once and for all.
shame.practice: Imagine that look on you again and finish silently: “It saw in me…, but I am also…” Say the second half slowly.

quote.text: Shame is shame of oneself before the Other.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

guilt.text: Sartre said a person is the sum of their actions — but the sum has not been added up yet. When guilt weighs on you, that is worth remembering. We answer for our actions because we are free: they cannot be blamed entirely on character or circumstances. But it’s important to distinguish responsibility from self-flagellation. Sartre criticized “bad faith” (mauvaise foi) — a self-deception in which we either pretend to be completely unfree or, on the contrary, reduce ourselves rigidly to a single act: “I’m just a bad person.” That is an escape too: you are not a thing with fixed properties, you are an ongoing choice. So guilt can become not a verdict but a point from which you decide how to live on. Acknowledging an act without reducing yourself to it — that is what honesty is.
guilt.practice: Write two sentences: “This is what I did…” and “Now I choose…” — and notice the gap between the act and you.

quote.text: Man is nothing else but what he makes of himself.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

envy.text: At the next table someone seems to be living a real life — and Sartre would explain why that picture is so convincing. Envy is unpleasant, but very human. Sartre described our relations with people through “the look”: another person easily becomes our yardstick, and we begin to see ourselves through their eyes. That means envy is a moment when someone else’s life seems “real” and complete, and yours seems insufficient. But Sartre would remind you: the other person is not a thing with a ready-made essence either — they too doubt and choose, and you see only the façade. And your own life is not yet settled; it is still taking shape. Beauvoir would add that many of our desires are shaped by our situation and by society’s expectations. You can take envy as a hint: what here is truly your own project, and what is a yardstick imposed on you?
envy.practice: Imagine living one ordinary Tuesday of the person you envy — with their doubts and fatigue. What from that day do you actually want?

emptiness.text: Sartre called man “a useless passion” — and drew from this that meaning can only be made, never found. If you feel hollow inside, existentialism knows that state firsthand. In Sartre’s novel Nausea, Antoine Roquentin suddenly sees the world stripped of any given meaning: things simply are, “superfluous,” there for nothing. It is an eerie experience, but the existentialists saw it as a starting point, not an end: if meaning isn’t given in advance, it can be created. “Existence precedes essence” — first we exist, and then we make someone of ourselves. Beauvoir stressed that meaning is born in “projects” — in what we do together with others and for the world. Emptiness doesn’t mean something is wrong with you; it means the ready-made meanings have stopped working. The new ones don’t have to be big: you can begin with something very small.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing not “because you have to” but because you decided to: move a cup, take a different route. Tell yourself: “This is my choice.”

confusion.text: “You are free, therefore choose — that is to say, invent,” Sartre told a confused student. When there are no ready answers, confusion is the most honest thing one can feel. Sartre described “abandonment”: there is no outside authority that will tell you how to live rightly. In his lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism he tells of a student who, during the war, didn’t know whether to leave and fight for the Free French or stay with his mother, for whom he was the only support. No moral system could decide for him, and all Sartre could do was hand him back his freedom. In other words, confusion is not a sign of stupidity but a sign that you are facing a real choice. Beauvoir would add that ambiguity is the normal condition of life, and you don’t need to wait for absolute clarity in order to act.
confusion.practice: Toss a coin with two options in mind and catch the moment while it’s in the air: which outcome are you already hoping for? That is your choice — the coin has nothing to do with it.

quote.text: You are free, therefore choose — that is to say, invent.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

fatigue.text: Beauvoir, who walked half of France on foot, knew that the body doesn’t argue with the will — it simply sets a limit. Exhaustion and burnout are not a lack of willpower. Existentialism is often associated with radical freedom, but Beauvoir clarified: freedom always exists in a “situation” — in a body, in circumstances, working conditions, relationships. The body is not an obstacle to freedom but its condition. In this light, fatigue speaks of the real limits of your situation, and acknowledging them is simply honest. If anything, it would be “bad faith” to pretend you are a tireless function. Sartre described a café waiter who plays “waiter” so diligently it is as if he were nothing but that role. You are not a role or a function. Allowing yourself to stop is also a free choice — perhaps the most honest one right now.
fatigue.practice: Picture the role you are playing hardest right now as a uniform — and mentally take it off, button by button. Sit for a minute without it.

boredom.text: Sunday in Bouville: Roquentin watches from a window as the townspeople promenade along the boulevard, and he has no idea how to fill the day. Boredom seems trivial, but the existentialists took it seriously. Sartre would probably say that boredom arises when the world stops responding to our “projects” — to what we are reaching toward: things are there, but they call us to nothing. Roquentin’s days drag, and his own life feels alien to him. But for existentialism this is not a verdict: if meaning isn’t built into the world in advance, boredom becomes a space in which you can ask what you yourself want. Beauvoir wrote of “transcendence” — the human capacity to go beyond what is given and reach toward something new. Perhaps boredom is a sign that it’s time to take a step somewhere else.
boredom.practice: Go out for five minutes and take a route you’ve never taken — purely out of curiosity, with no use to it. Notice one thing that called to you.

joy.text: August 1944, Paris liberated: Beauvoir later remembered those days as an explosion of pure joy. The existentialists were by no means philosophers of gloom alone. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described joy as a state in which we seem to possess what we desire immediately and entirely, without waiting for things to come together step by step. In The Ethics of Ambiguity Beauvoir argued against those who saw existentialism as a philosophy of despair: for her, freedom is not only a burden but also a source of the joy of existence, of creativity, friendship, the affirmation of life. So joy doesn’t need to be downplayed or postponed “until better times” — it is a legitimate way of being in the world. You can let yourself be glad without checking whether you’ve earned it and without waiting for a catch.
joy.practice: Say out loud what exactly is bringing you joy right now — in a full sentence, as if telling a friend some news.

love.text: In 1929 Sartre and Beauvoir made a pact: to be together without owning each other — and they argued about it all their lives. The tenderness you feel sits right at the heart of that argument. In Being and Nothingness Sartre described the contradiction of love: we want the other to choose us freely — and at the same time we want, as it were, to “possess” their freedom, which is impossible. Beauvoir looked for a way out of this impasse. In The Second Sex she wrote that authentic love should rest on the mutual recognition of two freedoms — a love in which neither dissolves into the other or becomes their shadow. That means tenderness is not a wish to appropriate but joy that the other is free and yet near. Love doesn’t cancel your freedom or demand that you sacrifice yourself. You can embrace it as a shared project of two people.
love.practice: Tell someone close one sentence about what you admire in their own choices — not in what they do for you.

gratitude.text: All her life Beauvoir remembered Zaza, the friend of her youth beside whom she first felt like herself, and she kept returning to her in her books. The warmth of gratitude sits perfectly well with existentialism. Beauvoir stressed that no one is free alone: my freedom becomes possible thanks to others — those who raised me, taught me, supported me, opened the world to me. Then gratitude is the recognition that your life is interwoven with other people’s freedoms and other people’s choices. This is not dependence or debt but the very “ambiguity” Beauvoir wrote about: we create ourselves and at the same time receive ourselves from others. Gratitude doesn’t diminish your independence. On the contrary, it shows what living connections your freedom grew out of — and lets you feel their warmth.
gratitude.practice: Send one person a short message: “My life would have gone differently without you — and here’s how.”

hope.text: Sartre’s last conversations, recorded in 1980, were published as Hope Now. If you are hoping for something, existentialism speaks about it honestly. Sartre warned against passive hope — waiting for everything to change by itself: a human being, he said, is their project and exists only to the extent that they realize themselves. But this isn’t a rejection of hope; it is an invitation to make it active. In his play The Flies, Orestes says that human life begins on the far side of despair: you don’t need guarantees in order to act. And in his last conversations in 1980, Sartre explicitly called hope part of what makes a human being human. In other words, hope is an open future in which your next step means something.
hope.practice: Take one tiny step right now toward what you hope for: look up the number, open the right page.

nostalgia.text: “I was born at four o’clock in the morning on 9 January 1908,” Beauvoir begins her memoirs. Reaching back toward the past is a tender and complicated feeling. For Sartre, the past is part of our “facticity”: it happened, it can’t be changed, and in a sense it becomes what we “are.” But for Sartre the meaning of the past is not fixed forever: it is determined by how we live now and what we choose next. The same event can turn out to be the beginning of a loss or the beginning of a new path — depending on what follows. In this light, nostalgia is not a prison but a dialogue: you long for what was valuable, and you can decide how that value will continue in your present life. In her many volumes of memoirs, Beauvoir showed how returning to the past helps you understand who you are becoming.
nostalgia.practice: Find an old photo from that time and look at it for a minute. What was valuable in it that could carry on today — even in a new form?

craving.text: A gambler who firmly resolved yesterday never to gamble again approaches the gaming table once more today — Sartre examines this example in Being and Nothingness without a hint of condemnation. A sharp “I want it right now” doesn’t make a person worse. The gambler discovers that yesterday’s resolution doesn’t work on its own — it lies in the past, and it has to be chosen anew, right now. Sartre saw in this the anguish (angoisse) of freedom. This doesn’t mean a craving is trivial and easy to defeat by willpower: Beauvoir reminded us that freedom always exists in a situation — with a body, a history, fatigue. But it does mean you don’t have to coincide with the wave of desire. In each new moment you decide again — and every “not now” is a real choice too, even if you have to repeat it a minute later.
craving.practice: Stand up, step three paces away from where it hit you, and say out loud: “This minute I choose…” — for instance, to step outside for some air.

addiction.text: For Sartre the key question is what we make of what has happened to us — and addiction is no exception. It is not a moral failure or a verdict on your character. Sartre distinguished “facticity” — everything already given: the body, the past, habits, circumstances — from “transcendence,” the capacity to go beyond what is given. A long-standing cycle of addiction is part of your facticity, and it weighs a great deal. But for Sartre a person never coincides completely with anything in themselves: you are not “an addict” the way a stone is a stone. Beauvoir added something important: freedom is not heroic in isolation; it is always realized together with others, in a situation where some things hinder and some people help. So leaving the cycle is not an act of a single super-will but the slow building of a different life “project” — one with room for people, support and time.
addiction.practice: If you feel like it, name out loud one person or one mutual-help group where this kind of cycle is understood from the inside. Just name it — nothing needs deciding now.

hangover.text: “The one who last night…” — Sartre showed how one phrase can turn a person into an object. The morning after drinking — heavy body, anxiety, shame — brings that trap very close. All of this deserves compassion, not judgment. Sartre described shame as experiencing yourself under “the look of the Other”: suddenly it seems you have turned into an object of someone else’s assessment, into “the one who last night…” But Sartre also has another thought: a person is never reducible to one act or one evening. We are not a thing with properties fixed once and for all but an existence that goes on. Beauvoir would add that we are “ambiguous” beings: there is vulnerability and freedom in us at the same time, and one doesn’t cancel the other. That means the morning after is not a verdict but one more point from which to carry on: calmly, without self-flagellation, taking care of yourself.
hangover.practice: Do one small thing today that looks after you rather than punishes you: a warm meal, a short walk, an honest message if one is needed.

euphoria.text: A world that suddenly seems within reach, as if by magic — Sartre knew that sensation and was in no hurry to devalue it. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre wrote that an emotion is a “magical” transformation of the world. In joy we seem to try to take possession of what we desire immediately and entirely, without waiting for the slow steps reality requires. Hence the feeling that everything is possible right now. Sartre didn’t consider this a mistake: this is how consciousness experiences the open fullness of the future. You can live through euphoria in all its brightness. And existentialism adds one thought that doesn’t spoil the moment but extends it: freedom lives not only in bursts but also in how the possibilities that opened up later become, step by step, your own projects.
euphoria.practice: Write down one possibility that has opened up for you now, and put the note away until tomorrow — let it wait for a calmer look.

crash.text: A moment ago the world was wide open, and now it is cramped and gray again — Sartre would describe this as the return of the “coefficient of adversity” of things. This is not your fault and not proof that the high was fake. Sartre spoke of the “coefficient of adversity” of things: the world doesn’t bend to our wishes instantly; everything has weight, distance, slowness. In the high this resistance seems to vanish, and in the drop it returns all at once, and the contrast feels unbearable. From Sartre’s point of view, emotion “magically” transforms the world, but reality then returns with its obstacles. This is not a defeat but an encounter with the real situation — the one in which freedom actually operates. You don’t need to demand a new take-off from yourself. You can take one step that matches today’s weight of the world.
crash.practice: Choose an action exactly the size of today’s strength — make the bed, wash one cup — and do it. Notice: the world has moved by one step.

panic.text: The world suddenly becomes one solid threat with no exit — Sartre described such moments without a hint of reproach. Your heart pounds, you can’t get enough air — it is genuinely frightening. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described how, in intense fear, consciousness, finding no way out through action, seems to fall into a “magical” world where the threat is everywhere at once. He stressed that emotion seizes the whole body and that consciousness gets caught in a trap it has set for itself: it believes in its own experience. Sartre saw this not as weakness but as an extreme attempt at self-protection. In this light, you don’t have to fight the wave; you can gently return from the “magical” world to the real one — through simple actions and sensations. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Pick up any solid object — keys, a cup — and feel its weight. Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and silently name what you are holding and where you are standing.

dread.text: Imagine a man who cannot die: Beauvoir made such a hero the center of her novel All Men Are Mortal (1946). When life’s finitude opens up and “what’s the point?” rises, her answer is unexpected. But in her novel All Men Are Mortal (1946), Simone de Beauvoir showed an unexpected side of this thought. Her hero Fosca is immortal — and precisely because of this nothing has any weight for him: love, work, choices can all be postponed, repeated, forgotten. Endlessness turns out to be not salvation but emptiness. Meaning, in Beauvoir’s view, is born exactly from the fact that time is not infinite: our actions matter because they are ours and cannot be repeated. Dread before the abyss is the flip side of how precious each particular life is, including yours. You don’t have to settle this question right away: you can let it remind you of what is dear to you.
dread.practice: Spend a minute looking at something that won’t happen in exactly this way again: the light in the window, a face, this evening. Tell yourself: “This is mine, and it happens once.”

fomo.text: “Hell is other people,” says a character in Sartre’s play No Exit — and the line knows a lot about the fear of missing out. It seems real life is happening elsewhere, and you’re too late. Sartre stressed that freedom always means choice, and choice means renunciation: in choosing one thing, I inevitably don’t live another. This is not a flaw in your life but the condition of every human life. Sartre also wrote a great deal about “the look of the Other”: we begin to see ourselves through other people’s eyes and to measure our lives against the picture others display. That line is often read as misanthropy, but Sartre himself explained: others become hell when we depend entirely on their judgment of us. So the fear of missing out is not the truth about your life but captivity to someone else’s gaze. Your life is where you choose.
fomo.practice: Put your phone face down and spend three minutes looking at what is right in front of you. Say: “This is where I am” — this is where your life is happening.

sleepless.text: At three in the morning, consciousness, as Sartre would put it, easily turns judge and starts passing verdicts. If you are awake and your thoughts are circling, that is not your fault. Sartre distinguished “pre-reflective” consciousness — when we simply live, act, see — from reflection, when consciousness turns back on itself. Within reflection he distinguished “pure” reflection, which simply sees clearly, from “impure” reflection, which starts to judge, pass verdicts, and mold a final image of oneself. At night, when you can’t act, reflection easily becomes “impure”: thoughts circle, past and future turn into sentences passed on you. That means nighttime conclusions are not the voice of truth but consciousness closed in on itself with no way out to the world. You don’t need to resolve them now: much of what seems final at night becomes an open question again by morning.
sleepless.practice: Tell the circling thought silently: “I’ll look at you in daylight.” Then feel the weight of the blanket and the coolness of the pillow — come back from reflection to simple presence.

betrayal.text: During the Occupation, Sartre and Beauvoir lived in a world where trust could cost a life, and they thought about treachery seriously. If you have been betrayed, your anger, confusion and grief are justified. In The Ethics of Ambiguity, Beauvoir wrote that one person’s freedom is inseparable from the freedom of others: we build our lives by leaning on one another. Trust is a decision to let another person into your own project, to make them part of your world. This is exactly where betrayal wounds: the other took advantage of that openness and treated you as a thing rather than as a free person. Then your pain is not naivety but evidence that you took the other person seriously. And importantly: betrayal speaks of the other person’s choice, not of your worth. Sartre insisted that each person answers for their own actions — and this action is not yours.
betrayal.practice: Speak aloud one value the betrayal touched — loyalty, openness, trust. Add: “It is still mine.”

jealousy.text: “The other is as much a center of the world as I am”: Beauvoir made this discovery not in a library but in her own love life. Jealousy is agonizing, and the existentialists knew it from more than books. Simone de Beauvoir’s first novel, She Came to Stay (1943), is built around jealousy in a love triangle and draws heavily on her own experience. Its heroine, Françoise, discovers this painfully. In Being and Nothingness Sartre explained why this hurts so much: we want the beloved to choose us freely, always, but the other’s freedom by definition cannot belong to us. So jealousy is not a sign of “bad” love but a collision with the fact that the beloved remains separate. In other words, you can accept it as the pain of that separateness — and ask yourself what you are actually missing.
jealousy.practice: For a minute, imagine the world through the eyes of the person you feel jealous about: they too are the center of their world. Then ask yourself: “What am I actually missing?”

resentment.text: A person can wait years for a single sentence — “I was wrong” — and the existentialists would explain why. Long-held resentment almost always has a real cause. Sartre and Beauvoir wrote a great deal about “recognition”: it is vital for a person that another acknowledge their freedom and dignity rather than treat them as a thing. In this light, resentment is recognition withheld: the expectation that the one who hurt you will someday understand and say “I was wrong.” This expectation is legitimate, but it quietly keeps you tied to that particular person’s gaze. Existentialism suggests not giving up your truth but ceasing to make someone else’s acknowledgment the only key to it. Recognition can come from other people and, above all, from yourself: an injustice remains an injustice even if the person who did it never admits it.
resentment.practice: Read aloud to yourself, slowly: “What happened to me was unfair, and my pain has its reasons.” Recognition starts with your own voice.

heartbreak.text: The Second Sex has a chapter called “The Woman in Love,” where Beauvoir writes about a love in which a person dissolves entirely. The pain of a broken heart shouldn’t be rushed. In The Second Sex, Beauvoir described how often in love a person — especially a woman, raised to do so — dissolves into the other: makes him the center of the world, sets aside her own projects, lives through his gaze. Then a breakup takes away not only the beloved but the very foundation of one’s own life. But her thought also offers comfort: your self does not disappear along with the relationship. Beneath the pain remain your own desires, friendships and pursuits, which you may not have thought about in a long time. You can grieve for as long as you need — and little by little reclaim your world.
heartbreak.practice: Give five minutes today to something that was yours before this relationship: a song, a route, a book, a craft.

impostor.text: Sartre’s waiter moves a little too precisely and bows a little too eagerly — as if he were “playing” at being a waiter. The scene is from Being and Nothingness, and it is familiar to anyone haunted by the sense of “I’m about to be found out.” Sartre shows that we all do this in one way or another: no one is their role the way a table is a table. A doctor, a teacher, a manager — each performs a role that never fully coincides with them. So feeling like an impostor is not proof that you are worse than others but an honest sense of the gap between person and role that everyone has. The only difference is that you notice it. Your competence lives in your actions, not in perfectly coinciding with a role.
impostor.practice: Recall one thing you did well in this role and tell someone about it in a single sentence — without qualifiers.

self_hatred.text: The inner critic says “that’s what you are” in a judge’s voice, and Sartre spent his life arguing with exactly that tone. When you hate yourself, the verdict sounds like the truth. But existentialism offers an important objection. Sartre counted as “bad faith” (mauvaise foi), among other things, the attempt to define oneself once and for all, like a thing: “that’s just what I am,” “I’m worthless.” A human being, for Sartre, never coincides with anyone’s verdict — not even their own. In his book on the writer Jean Genet, Sartre showed how a boy whom adults branded a thief first accepted this alien word as his fate and then turned it into literature — made of it something his own. The critic’s voice is often a look from someone else, absorbed long ago. That means its verdict is not final: you are bigger than any label.
self_hatred.practice: Voice the label your inner critic uses, and then one thing you did that doesn’t fit it. Say: “That is me too.”

quote.text: What is important is not what people make of us, but what we ourselves make of what they have made of us.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

helplessness.text: Beauvoir once argued with Sartre: is a woman shut away in a harem as free as someone who can walk out? She insisted she was not — and she would have understood your powerlessness. Sartre is often portrayed as the champion of boundless freedom, but Beauvoir corrected this: freedom always exists in a situation — with a body, money, history, other people’s power. In The Ethics of Ambiguity she wrote that there are situations in which a person’s possibilities really are taken away, and this is not their fault but an injustice. Then your powerlessness may honestly reflect real constraints rather than personal weakness. But existentialism adds: even in a tight situation there remains the freedom of your stance — how to understand what has happened, what to lean on, whom to join with. Beauvoir stressed that freedom grows together with others: what is impossible alone sometimes becomes possible alongside someone.
helplessness.practice: Divide a page in half: on the left, what is currently beyond your control; on the right, one small thing where you still have a choice, even if only in how you relate to what is happening.

procrastination.text: The task lies on the desk, and consciousness suddenly finds a thousand reasons to consider it boring — Sartre would call this a small act of sorcery. It almost never comes down to laziness. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre wrote that when the path of action seems too difficult, consciousness looks for a “magical” way out: instead of changing the world, it changes how the world is perceived. Like the fox in the fable who declares the grapes he can’t reach to be sour, we suddenly find the task boring, unimportant or frightening — and putting it off feels like relief. In other words, procrastination is not a vice but a form of self-protection when the task feels like a wall. You don’t have to choose to “do everything.” It is enough to choose a first step so small that the wall turns into a road.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and do only the very first step — open the file, take out the notebook. When the timer rings, you may stop.

uprooted.text: For years Sartre and Beauvoir lived in hotels — home, for them, was more a matter of what they did than of a place. Losing your familiar supports after a move or emigration runs deep. Sartre described human life through the notion of “situation”: place, language, surroundings are not scenery but that within which our projects take shape. Beauvoir would remind you that this is not only a personal trial: a move is often tied to circumstances beyond a person’s control, and feeling lost is an honest response to them. But Sartre stressed something else as well: the meaning of a place is not given in advance. It becomes “mine” through what I do in it, whom I connect with, where I go. In this light, your former home remains part of your story, while the new one is still being built — by your choices.
uprooted.practice: Take a walk around your new place and choose one spot — a bench, a window, a corner — that from today on you will count as yours.

overload.text: A bus queue on the Place Saint-Germain: people stand side by side but are connected only by waiting for the same thing — this is how the later Sartre, in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, described “seriality.” An endless feed is exhausting, and it isn’t about your weakness. Everyone there is interchangeable and alone among others. The feed creates a similar seriality: millions of people look at the same thing, but each alone, and the rhythm is set by the stream rather than by their own projects. Being worn out by this is how a freedom responds when it is left no room. Existentialism doesn’t ask you to renounce the world, but it reminds you: attention is also a choice, and you can take it back, even if only for a few minutes.
overload.practice: Close all your tabs and sit for two minutes without reading anything. Then ask: “What do I myself want to know?” — and turn to that alone.

unreality.text: A tram, a seat, and the word “seat” that suddenly won’t settle on the object — Sartre wrote this scene in Nausea. If it feels as though everything around you, or you yourself, is not quite real, that is strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. Things become alien, as if seen for the first time. Sartre described this without any diagnosis — as a moment when the familiar web of names and meanings loosens. It is frightening, but for Sartre it shows that the ordinary “normality” of the world rests on our participation: we are constantly giving things meaning. So unreality is not the disappearance of the world but a temporary loosening of that bond, and it is restored through action and contact.
unreality.practice: Pick up a simple object, name it out loud, and do something with it: pour water into a glass, move a book. Let the action make the thing familiar again.

awe.text: Beauvoir would set off alone into the mountains of Provence for a whole day — in her memoir The Prime of Life she described these hikes with delight, walking for hours, captivated by the open space. The existentialists are often pictured as gloomy, but awe before the vast was well known to them. For her this was the joy of freedom meeting the world. In What Is Literature? Sartre wrote that the human being is the one through whom being is “revealed”: mountains and sea do not wait for us, yet it is in the human gaze that their grandeur unfolds. That means awe is the moment when your freedom meets something greater than itself and feels not diminished but enlarged. It doesn’t need to be explained or put to use: it is enough to let yourself be a witness.
awe.practice: Go to a window or step outside and spend a minute looking at the largest thing in view: the sky, a tree, a building. Say to yourself: “I am a witness.”

relief.text: A door that was locked a moment ago is suddenly open — and the whole room, Sartre would say, has changed. Relief is worth living through rather than skipping past. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described how an emotion changes the whole face of the world: in anxiety everything presses and threatens, and when the threat passes, the world again becomes a place where one can act. Relief is exactly such a transition — from “nothing is possible” to “it’s possible again.” From Beauvoir’s point of view one might add that relief always comes in a concrete situation, after a concrete strain, and honestly reflects how much you have endured. So relief is not a trifle, nor a cue to jump straight into the next thing. It is the moment when freedom feels space around itself again. Let yourself notice it and stay in it a little.
relief.practice: Take a deep breath and a slow exhale, straighten your shoulders, and name out loud one thing that has become possible again.

calm.text: Beauvoir loved long evenings of conversation and slow walks — her philosophy of freedom did not rule out idleness. Peace needs no justification. It might seem that a philosophy of freedom and responsibility leaves no room for rest. But in The Ethics of Ambiguity Beauvoir criticized “the serious man” — the one who subordinates life to abstract goals and never lets himself simply be. Freedom, in her view, exists not for the sake of an endless race but for the sake of life itself, with room in it for joy, play, unhurriedness. In other words, calm is neither an escape from responsibility nor “empty” time. It is one form of freedom: you allow yourself to live, not only to achieve. You don’t need to earn it — you can simply choose to stay in it.
calm.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now I choose not to achieve anything” — and sit like that for a couple of minutes, noticing what it feels like.

inspiration.text: “To write is to make an appeal to the reader,” Sartre argued in What Is Literature? (1948). When inspiration takes hold of you, that joyful, living state is worth cherishing. For him creative work is an “appeal” to the freedom of another: the writer creates a text, but it comes alive only when a reader freely responds. In this light, inspiration is not a mysterious gift sent from outside but a moment when your freedom senses that it can address the world and other people. Beauvoir wrote all her life — novels, essays, memoirs — and saw writing as a way of making sense of her situation and sharing it with others. Inspiration doesn’t have to become a masterpiece to be real. It is an invitation: you can add to the world something that wouldn’t be there without you.
inspiration.practice: Write one opening sentence addressed to a particular person — even an imagined one — for whom the thing you want to create is meant.

schadenfreude.text: For a moment someone else is under the gaze instead of you — Sartre would explain why that brings relief. Schadenfreude is awkward to admit, but it says nothing final about you. Sartre described how we live under “the look of the Other”: others see us, assess us, and we constantly feel ourselves in their eyes. Under this strain, someone else’s success can feel like a threat, and someone else’s failure like a brief respite: for a moment, it’s not us being judged. Schadenfreude is not an “evil essence” — all the more so since, for Sartre, a person has no essence in advance: we define ourselves by what we do. The feeling flared up — that’s a fact, but what you make of it is up to you. You can simply notice it and ask where you are currently feeling judged.
schadenfreude.practice: Finish the sentence, silently or on paper: “Their failure made me feel better because I’m afraid of being judged as…”

contempt.text: In the Bouville museum Roquentin studies the portraits of the town’s smug founding fathers and calls them “bastards.” If you are looking at someone with contempt right now, don’t rush to judge yourself: Sartre knew this cold feeling well. But he also saw the other side: in Anti-Semite and Jew he showed how contempt for others can serve as a way of avoiding one’s own freedom and uncertainty — leaning on someone else’s “baseness” in order to feel solid. So it helps to ask: is the contempt protecting your worth — or helping you avoid looking at something in yourself? Both answers are possible, and both deserve an honest look.
contempt.practice: Ask yourself quietly: “Looking at this person, what do I not want to be?” — and stay with the answer for a minute without judging it.

disgust.text: The root of a chestnut tree in the public garden suddenly seems to Roquentin viscous, superfluous, sickeningly real. Disgust is a strong, almost bodily feeling, and there’s no need to argue with it. Sartre’s novel Nausea is devoted entirely to a similar experience: the hero suddenly feels sick at the very existence of things — the root of a chestnut tree, a glass of beer, his own hand. Everything seems superfluous, viscous, obtrusively present. For Sartre this was a discovery: the world is not obliged to have a ready-made meaning, and disgust is an encounter with this naked contingency. That means disgust at a situation, at people or at yourself can be understood as a moment when familiar meanings fall away. It’s unpleasant, but it’s also honest. The novel ends not in despair but with a faint hope: the hero hears a song and thinks about creating something of his own.
disgust.practice: Step away from what disgusts you, take a few slow breaths out, and look at something pleasant. Then ask: “What meaning am I missing here?”

quote.text: The Nausea is not inside me: I feel it out there in the wall, in the suspenders, everywhere around me.
quote.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

revenge.text: In the winter of 1945 Beauvoir sat in the courtroom at the trial of the collaborator Brasillach, trying to understand what she really wanted — justice or retribution. When you have been hurt, a force rises in you demanding justice. In her essay “An Eye for an Eye” (1946), Simone de Beauvoir examined this feeling seriously, without condemning it. She wrote that there is a deep human meaning in revenge: we want the one who wronged us to recognize that we are free people, not things that can be treated any way at all. But Beauvoir also saw the tragedy of revenge: recognition cannot be wrested by force, and pain inflicted in return doesn’t give back what was taken. Then your wish is a demand for respect for your freedom. You can look for ways that affirm this freedom rather than multiply harm.
revenge.practice: Write: “I want them to understand that I…” What recognition do you actually need?

anger_at_loved.text: If we extend Sartre’s thought, emotions flare most often where there is no walking away — and it is hardest of all to walk away from those we love. Flaring up at a partner, parents or children, and the shame afterward, don’t make you a bad person. In his Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, Sartre described emotions as “magical” behavior: when a situation becomes unbearable and there is no direct way out, consciousness tries to change the world by the force of feeling. With loved ones this happens especially often, because it’s with them that we most often hit a dead end: fatigue, recurring conflicts, being unable to walk away. Beauvoir would add that freedom is always embodied in a concrete situation — in a shortage of strength, time, support. In other words, an outburst is a signal of a dead end, not the truth about your love.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, step into another room for a minute and take five slow breaths out. Ask: “What dead end was I in?” — and find one small way out.

ambivalence.text: Beauvoir titled her book The Ethics of Ambiguity, holding ambiguity to be not a defect but the very essence of human existence. For someone who cherishes a person and at the same time can’t stand them, the title is almost a comfort: this happens, and it is deeply human. We are free and limited at once, connected to others and separate, we love and we want independence. Beauvoir criticized attempts to flee this ambiguity — to make everything unequivocal, “correct,” settled once and for all. In this light, mixed feelings toward someone close are not a sign of false love but an honest reflection of the fact that relationships between two free people are inevitably double-edged. You don’t have to choose one feeling; you can live acknowledging both.
ambivalence.practice: Say silently, not to them: “I love you, and at the same time it’s hard for me when you…” Let both halves of the sentence sound equally loud.

guilty_relief.text: A Very Easy Death is a book in which Beauvoir hid none of her feelings. If relief has come after a breakup, a departure or a loved one’s long illness, and sharp guilt has followed it, know this: relief doesn’t cancel love. In A Very Easy Death (1964), Simone de Beauvoir described with rare honesty the last weeks of her mother’s life — and how contradictory her own feelings were: tenderness, exhaustion, anger, pity. She didn’t try to make them “proper.” Her “ethics of ambiguity” suggests that human feelings are rarely pure, and honesty matters more than meeting expectations. Your relief is one of the voices inside you, alongside grief and love. It speaks of how much you were carrying, not of how little you loved.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down three feelings you have right now toward this person and this situation. Let all three stay on the page.

indifference.text: “The spirit of seriousness” — that is what Sartre and Beauvoir called the belief that values and correct reactions are given in advance, like laws of nature, and that we are obliged to conform to them. If there is only silence inside where you “ought” to be moved, it’s frightening, but it doesn’t make you heartless — nothing shameful has happened to you. For the existentialists there is no ready-made list of what one is “supposed” to feel. So your indifference is not a broken rule but a fact of your state that can be honestly acknowledged. Sartre showed that emotions are ways of responding to a situation; sometimes silence is also a response — to exhaustion or overload, for example. Honestly acknowledging it is already a beginning. Meaning doesn’t have to appear on demand.
indifference.practice: Sit for two minutes with this silence, without trying to feel “the proper way.” Just note: “This is how it is right now.”

escape.text: At twenty-one Beauvoir left her parents’ home and rented a room from her grandmother, so as not to live by someone else’s script. The urge to drop everything says a lot about you. Sartre held that “existence precedes essence”: you don’t have to coincide forever with the role of waiter, manager, “good daughter.” A role is not your nature but something you once chose or accepted. In the essay Pyrrhus and Cineas, Beauvoir tells of a king who plans to conquer the whole world so that he can rest afterward — and of an adviser who asks: why not rest right now? She shows that a human being always reaches beyond what is. That means the urge to escape is a sign of a freedom that doesn’t fit inside the frame. You don’t need to tear everything down at once: first you can ask where exactly that freedom is pulling you.
escape.practice: Imagine one ordinary day in which you are not reducible to your role. What would be in it? Find one small thing in that day that is possible this very week.

forbidden_attraction.text: A woman on a date leaves her hand in her companion’s and acts as if nothing is happening — this is how Sartre, in Being and Nothingness, shows us hiding from our own choice. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” is unsettling, but by itself it decides nothing and doesn’t define you. Sartre called this kind of self-deception “bad faith.” Then it is more honest to acknowledge the attraction than to pretend it isn’t there. Acknowledging it doesn’t commit you to any action. It simply gives you back clarity: this is what I feel, and I am the one who decides how to live with it. Freedom begins with the truth about yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Put a hand on your chest and tell yourself without judgment: “Yes, I feel this.” Notice how the tension changes when you don’t have to pretend.

social_anxiety.text: A café where it feels as if everyone is looking at you is the perfect setting for Sartre’s philosophy. Being afraid of people and their judgment is exhausting, and you are not alone in it. Sartre described “the look of the Other”: when we are looked at, we suddenly feel ourselves to be an object under assessment, and we can’t control how we are seen. This really is unsettling — Sartre didn’t pretend it was easy. But he also showed that the other sees only one side, a momentary snapshot, while you remain a freedom that goes on. Beauvoir would add that others live under someone’s gaze too — and that people’s freedoms are bound up with each other, not only set against each other. In other words, the person you feel shy in front of is most likely a little afraid of your gaze as well.
social_anxiety.practice: In a crowded place, look at two or three strangers and notice: each of them is under someone’s gaze too and may be a little nervous. How does your breathing change?

uncertainty.text: Sartre said that a human being “projects” themselves into a future that does not yet exist — like a bridge built while you are already walking across it. Not knowing is draining: you long for something solid, and there isn’t anything. Sartre described “anguish” as the feeling that comes when we become aware of our freedom: nothing guarantees in advance what will happen, and no rule will decide for us. He didn’t pretend this was pleasant. But here, too, lies a possibility: since the future isn’t written, our actions truly mean something. Beauvoir stressed that freedom always exists in a concrete situation — with limitations that need to be honestly taken into account. In this light, uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space for choice. You don’t have to see the whole road: the next step, chosen by you, is enough.
uncertainty.practice: Say one sentence to someone: “I don’t know how it will turn out, but today I choose…” — and finish it.

waiting.text: Pyrrhus prepares to conquer the whole world so that he can rest afterward, and his adviser asks why not rest now — Beauvoir examined this dispute in her essay Pyrrhus and Cineas. Waiting for results, an answer, news can stretch out agonizingly. Sartre described the human being as a creature always reaching forward, toward its possibilities: we live by “projecting” ourselves into the future. That’s why waiting is so hard: the future we reach toward depends on someone else’s decision, and we freeze. In Pyrrhus and Cineas, Beauvoir reflected that a person cannot live only for what will come “later”: the present must have meaning too. You don’t have to hand all your time over to waiting. Until the decision arrives, you remain a freedom that can choose how to live today.
waiting.practice: Right now, do one thing that is meaningful regardless of the answer: water a plant, call a friend, make tea.

regret.text: The past, for Sartre, is like a sentence whose ending hasn’t been written: the words can’t be changed, but their meaning depends on the ones that follow. Regret over what you did or didn’t do speaks of what matters to you. Sartre held that the past is part of our “facticity”: it happened, and it can’t be changed. But for Sartre the meaning of the past is not closed. It is determined by what we do now: the same event can become the end of a road or a turn toward something new — depending on what you choose today. So regret is not only a verdict but also material. You don’t have to be the person who once made a mistake: you are choosing yourself anew all the time. You can ask not “why did I do that?” but “what will I make of it now?”
regret.practice: Ask yourself not “why did I do that?” but “what will I make of it now?” — and answer out loud in one sentence.

longing.text: Sartre walks into a café where he has arranged to meet his friend Pierre, a quarter of an hour late — and Pierre isn’t there. This scene from Being and Nothingness describes very precisely what it is to long for a particular person. The whole café — the tables, the faces, the smoke — becomes a background for this absence: he sees not the café but “not-Pierre.” Sartre showed that absence is not emptiness but a special kind of presence that colors the whole world. That means longing is the way a beloved person goes on being in your world: through their absence. It is a sign of how much they have become part of your meanings. You don’t have to drive this feeling away; you can carry it gently.
longing.practice: Notice today the place or moment where this person’s absence is felt most strongly. Pause there for a minute and silently say hello to them.

world_pain.text: Sartre read the newspapers almost every day and signed appeals — he did not know how to turn away from the world. Grim news, violence and injustice wound you too, and that speaks of your capacity for compassion. Sartre wrote that in choosing ourselves we are, in a sense, choosing an image of humanity as a whole, and so we are responsible not only for ourselves. That can seem like an unbearable weight. But Beauvoir clarified: freedom is always concrete and embodied in a situation. We cannot carry the whole world, but we can act where we are — support a person nearby, do what is within our power. Your pain is a sign of your connection with others. It can be turned into concrete care without drowning in an endless stream of news. Protecting your strength is also part of responsibility.
world_pain.practice: This week, do one concrete thing within your means — support someone nearby, for example — and then give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: You stand under someone’s gaze, and that gaze reaches a decision without you — this is how Sartre described the encounter with the Other. When you have been turned away, the wound is deep, and that is natural. Sartre described in detail how we depend on the look of the Other: another person can see in us what we don’t see in ourselves, and we have no power over their judgment. That is exactly why rejection hits so hard: another freedom has said “no,” and we can’t talk it round. But there is also a liberating thought here: someone else’s view is their choice, not the final truth about you. You are not reducible to how one person saw you. For Sartre, a human being has no ready-made essence that someone could conclusively assess. You go on creating yourself through your actions.
rejection.practice: Tell someone close one thing about yourself that the person who turned you down never got to see.

abandonment.text: “Abandonment” is one of Sartre’s key words: he used it for the position of every human being, to whom no one above has handed instructions. The fear of being left sounds especially sharp in this word, and it deserves gentleness. It sounds cold, but Beauvoir added something important: one person’s freedom is always bound up with the freedom of others; we need each other for our lives to have meaning. The fear of being abandoned is an acute experience of that dependence. In this light, you can acknowledge: the other person is free, and their presence can’t be guaranteed. That hurts. But a bond that rests on freedom rather than control is the most valuable kind. And you are not defenseless: you too have the freedom to build connections.
abandonment.practice: Strengthen one connection today with a small step — a message, a call, a word of thanks.

unrequited.text: The lover, for Sartre, wants to become the whole world for the other — and that is his unavoidable trouble. When love goes unanswered, the pain is real. Sartre was rather bleak in his account of love: in Being and Nothingness he showed that the lover wants to become everything to the other, but the other’s freedom always slips away — it can’t be appropriated. Beauvoir saw it differently: in The Second Sex she wrote that authentic love is built on the mutual recognition of two freedoms. Love going unreturned is not your failure but an encounter with another person’s freedom, which no strength of feeling can change. You haven’t become any less because you weren’t chosen. Your capacity to love is yours, and it stays with you.
unrequited.practice: Read to yourself slowly, under your breath: “They are free not to love me. I am free to remain myself.”

quote.text: Genuine love ought to be founded on the mutual recognition of two liberties.
quote.author: Simone de Beauvoir

humiliation.text: “What matters is not what has been made of us, but what we ourselves make of what has been made of us,” Sartre wrote. Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences, and it is not your fault that you went through it. Sartre described how the look of the Other can turn us into an object — a “frozen” image over which we have no power. Humiliation is the extreme form of this: you are not merely seen but reduced to something low. All her life Beauvoir wrote about how people are deprived of freedom by being made “other,” made into objects. So humiliation is not the truth about you but an act by someone who refused you recognition. Your freedom hasn’t disappeared — it is wounded, but it goes on.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, straighten your back and plant both feet on the floor. Ask yourself: “What do I want to make of what was done to me?” — and answer in one word.

body_shame.text: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” — and in the same way, Beauvoir showed, no one is born believing their body is “not right.” It is a common and painful feeling. In The Second Sex, Simone de Beauvoir showed that our relationship to our body is largely created by society: by looks, standards and expectations we absorb from childhood. The image of the “right” body is not nature but a cultural script. Sartre would add that we experience the body as a “body-for-others”: we see ourselves through other people’s eyes. That means shame about your body is not the truth about you but a reflection of someone else’s gaze. Little by little, you can reclaim your body as your way of living rather than an object of assessment.
body_shame.practice: Rest your palms on your shoulders and feel what this body is doing for you right now: breathing, holding you up, keeping you warm. One minute — no judgment, just attention to its work.

quote.text: …the body is not a thing, it is a situation.
quote.author: Simone de Beauvoir

illness.text: Toward the end of his life Sartre went almost blind and kept working — dictating and listening as friends read to him. When your body lets you down, the ground goes out from under you. It is hard, and you have every right to grieve. In Being and Nothingness, Sartre described the body not as an object we own but as that through which we are in the world at all. He gave an example: a person’s eyes ache while reading — and the pain is not separate from the reading; it colors the very lines on the page. Beauvoir stressed that freedom always exists in a situation, and illness is a situation too, not the end of freedom. Then you remain a person who chooses how to live these days, even if the range of choice has narrowed. Sometimes freedom lies simply in how you treat yourself today.
illness.practice: Make one small decision yourself today — what to read, whom to talk to, how to rest — and tell yourself: “I chose this.”

pride.text: “Man is nothing else but the sum of his actions,” Sartre said in his famous 1945 lecture. Pride in what you have done is a healthy and well-earned feeling, and there is no need to hurry to hide it. In other words, pride in an outcome is recognizing yourself in your own action: this is what I chose, this is what I created. It is the opposite of “bad faith,” in which we hide from our freedom. Beauvoir warned against only one thing — turning achievements into a frozen idol, into “the spirit of seriousness,” where the result becomes more important than the living person. But pride as joy in what you have done is an acknowledgment of your own freedom in action. Let yourself enjoy this moment.
pride.practice: Say out loud what you did and what choice lay behind it. Say: “This is mine.”

melancholy.text: A record playing in a café — on the last pages of Nausea Sartre gives his exhausted hero a moment of bright sadness, where sorrow is mixed with tenderness. It doesn’t need “fixing.” The hero, worn out by meaninglessness, sits listening to an old jazz song, “Some of These Days.” The melody is sad, but it has a purity and necessity that the chaos of things lacks. The hero feels a faint hope: perhaps he, too, could create something like it. In this light, melancholy may be not a decline but a special sensitivity to the beauty of what passes. Sartre and Beauvoir held that we create meaning ourselves — and bright sadness often becomes the beginning of such creation.
melancholy.practice: Listen to one song that matches your mood, all the way to the end, without doing anything else at the same time.
